field_commentary.value: シテの漁翁は、夕浪が引いて夜となり、また朝になると言って、朝に掛けて「朝倉」を導く。そして「朝倉や。木の丸殿にあらばこそ」と天智天皇の歌「朝倉やきのまろどのにわがをれば名のりをしつつ行くはたが子ぞ」（『新古今集』168番）を想起させる回答をする。「きのまろどの」は百済出兵のために九州朝倉に仮に作られた木づくりの質素な天皇の住まい。『新古今集』168番の和歌は、母・斉明天皇の喪に服している皇太子時代の天智天皇の歌で、朝倉にある木の丸御殿にいると、名前を名乗っていく子がいるが、あれは誰の子どもなのだ？という意味。質素な宮殿での警備のために通る人には必ず名乗らせていたという伝承がある（『十訓抄』）。この歌の「名のりをしつつ」の引用から、漁翁は「名のりをしても行かまし」と言う。つまり、「もしここが朝倉にある木の丸殿であるなら必ず名のりをするが、今は名のならずにおこう」と我が身を明かさず、はぐらかす。朝倉は「名を明かす」を導く地名で、もし今朝倉にいるなら我が名を名乗るが、漁翁がいる場所は朝倉ではないので名前は明かさないのである。

field_commentary_eng.value:
The old fisherman as shite, uses the fact that the evening wave recedes into the night and returns back in the morning to play on the word "asa" (morning) and introduce the place name Asakura. He responds to the monk saying "Asakura! If only I were at Ki no Marodono", referring to the famous poem by Emperor Tenji (Shin Kokin Wakashū #168) that translates as: "As I am at Ki no Marodono Palace in Asakura,
A child walks by, calling out their name—
Whose child might it be?" "Ki no marodono" refers to the simple wooden residence which was built to serve as an imperial residence during Emperor Tenji's military expedition to Baekje (on the Korean Peninsula) in Asakura, Kyushu. The poem was written by Emperor Tenji while he was crown prince, mourning his mother, Empress Saimei, at Asakura. In the poem he expresses his curiosity towards the child passing by, wondering who they may be, as each person was required to announce their name when passing by the palace, a custom that is recorded in the Jikkinshō. Playing off the line in the poem “calling out one’s name”, the old fisherman responds, "If this were the Ki no Marudono at Asakura, I would indeed announce my name." In other words, he implies that if they were at Asakura, he would declare his name, but as they are not, he will leave his identity ambiguous and avoid revealing it. Although Asakura is a place that invites "declaring one's name," here, they are not in Asakura, so he refrains from doing so.

field_commentary.value: 杉村弾正少弼（シテ）は、天智天皇が筑紫朝倉の里に籠っていたことに触れ、「朝倉の里では人は必ずその名を名のるべし」という綸言の和歌「朝倉やきのまろどのにわがをれば名のりをしつつ行くはたが子ぞ」（『新古今集』168番）を天智天皇が詠んだことにちなみ、和歌浦がある紀伊国粉川においても本名を名のろうと言う。「きのまろどの」は百済出兵のために九州朝倉に仮に作られた木づくりの質素な天皇の住まい。『新古今集』168番歌は、母・斉明天皇の喪に服している皇太子時代の天智天皇の歌で、朝倉にある木の丸御殿にいると、名前を名乗っていく子がいるが、あれは誰の子どもなのだ？という意味。朝倉は「名を明かす」語を導く地名となっており、本曲の舞台は朝倉ではないが、和歌で名を明かすように命じたことから、和歌の浦と名のついたこの場所なので、和歌の言葉に裏はない（「和歌の浦波」をかける）、つまり和歌の言葉は絶対であり、名乗らないでおくことはできないと言う。

field_commentary_eng.value:
In his kusemai dance, Sugimura Danjō no Shōhitsu alludes to Emperor Tenji’s time in seclusion at the village of Asakura in Tsukushi and references the Jikkinshō "in Asakura, all must announce their name." He cites the poem by Emperor Tenji, "As I am at Ki no Marodono Palace in Asakura, a child walks by, calling out their name—Whose child might it be?" (Shin Kokin Wakashū #168)
Inspired by this precedent, Sugimura declares that he, too, will reveal his true name here in Kokawa, in Kii Province, where Wakanoura Bay lies.
The "Ki no Marodono" mentioned in the poem refers to the simple wooden residence which was built to serve as an imperial residence during Emperor Tenji's military expedition to Baekje (on the Korean Peninsula) in Asakura, Kyushu.  The poem was composed by Emperor Tenji, then Crown Prince, while in mourning for his mother, Empress Saimei. In the poem, he reflects on his time at Ki no Marodono in Asakura, wondering whose child might be passing by, calling out their name, as each person was required to announce their name when passing the palace. Asakura thus became a place associated with "revealing one’s name."
Though the setting of this story is not Asakura, Sugimura draws on the poem’s command to "reveal one’s name" to proclaim that, here at Wakanoura, which contains "waka" (Japanese poetry), he will honor the command of the poem. By a wordplay on "Wakanoura waves" (interpreted as the honesty of poetry), he implies that the words of poetry are absolute; therefore, he cannot remain without announcing his name.

field_scene_description.value: 杉村弾正少弼(シテ)は、紀州粉川寺にて、人を泊めてはいけない日に宿を所望し断られる。しかし、稚児梅夜叉(子方)の機転で、仮名字（偽名）を名乗って宿を得る。後日、梅夜叉に会うために再び寺を訪れたところ、寺の住職（ワキ）に、本当の名前を尋ねられたので、仮名字に関する曲舞を舞った後に答えようと言い、曲舞〔くせまい〕を謡う。曲舞のなかで、天智天皇が筑紫朝倉の里に籠っていたことに触れ、朝倉の里では、人は必ずその名を名のることになっていたというから、ここ粉河寺でも、自分も本名を名乗ろうと言う。

field_scene_description_eng.value:
Sugimura Danjō (the shite) arrives at Kokawadera Temple in Kii Province seeking accommodation but is refused, as it is a day when guests are not permitted. However, thanks to the cleverness of a page named Ume no Yasha (the kokata), he is allowed to stay under the assumed name. Later, when he revisits the temple to see Ume no Yasha again, the temple’s head priest (the waki) asks him for his true name. Sugimura replies that he will reveal his real name after performing a kusemai dance on the theme of assumed names, and then begins his dance.
During the kusemai, he references Emperor Tenji’s time in seclusion in the village of Asakura in Tsukushi, noting how, in Asakura, all were required to announce their names. Drawing a parallel, he declares that he too will now reveal his true name here at Kokawadera.

field_commentary.value: 杉村弾正少弼は、自分の本名を名のるために、「名乗る」にちなんだ天智天皇の歌「朝倉やきのまろどのにわがをれば名のりをしつつ行くはたが子ぞ」（『新古今集』168番）を引用して謡う。そのために、天智天皇が筑紫朝倉の里に籠っていたことに触れる。『新古今集』168番にいう「きのまろどの」は百済出兵のために九州朝倉に仮に作られた木づくりの質素な天皇の住まいで、母・斉明天皇の喪に服している皇太子時代の天智天皇が、朝倉にある木の丸御殿にいると、名前を名乗っていく子がいるが、あれは誰の子どもなのだ？と詠んだ和歌。

field_commentary_eng.value: Sugimura Danjō no Shōhitsu, in order to announce his real name, recites the poem by Emperor Tenji that refers to "calling out one's name": "As I am at Ki no Marodono Palace in Asakura, A child walks by, calling out their name—Whose child might it be?" ( Shin Kokin Wakashū #168) In doing so, he references Emperor Tenji’s time spent secluded in the village of Asakura in Tsukushi. The "Ki no Marodono" refers to the simple wooden residence which was built to serve as an imperial residence during Emperor Tenji's military expedition to Baekje (on the Korean Peninsula) in Asakura, Kyushu. This poem was composed by Emperor Tenji, then Crown Prince, while in mourning for his mother, Empress Saimei. In the poem, he reflects on his time at Ki no Marodono in Asakura, wondering whose child might be passing by, calling out their name.

field_context.value:
ワキ詞「重ねて御登山祝着申し候。以前は仮名字にて御出の由承り候。此度は誠の御名字を御名乗り候へ。

シテ「仮名字につきて面白き曲舞の候ふ程に諷ひ。その時名宣り候ふべし。

サシ「吉野山の花見の行幸には。妹背の中を離れ。

地「須磨明石の月に休らふとても。三年の日数を徒らに過し。その後筑紫筑前に下り。朝倉の里と云ふ処に。暫く御座をなし給ふ。

field_scene_description.value: 杉村弾正(シテ)は、紀州粉川寺にて、人を泊めてはいけない日に宿を所望し断られる。しかし、稚児梅夜叉(子方)の機転で、仮名字（偽名）を名乗って宿を得る。後日、梅夜叉に会うために再び寺を訪れたところ、寺の住職（ワキ）に、本当の名前を尋ねられたので、仮名字に関する曲舞を舞った後に答えようと言い、曲舞〔くせまい〕を謡う場面。曲舞の内で、天智天皇が筑紫朝倉の里に籠っていたことに触れている。

field_scene_description_eng.value: On a day when people are not allowed to stay overnight at Kokawa-ji Temple in Kii province, Sugimura Danjō (shite) asks for lodging but is refused. However, with the help of the young boy Umeyasha (kokata), he is able to obtain accommodation under a false name. Later, when he visits the temple again to see Umeyasha, the temple priest (waki) asks him about his real name, Danjō tells him that he will answer him after he has danced (and sung) a Kusemai about his pseudonym. In this scene he sings the Kusemai.
